concept.title: Headings
concept.abstract: This section covers the Heading style in HTML — its role as the primary structural mechanism that organizes a document's content into a named, hierarchical sequence of sections — and four scenarios: headings applied in correct sequential order, a heading level skipped in the hierarchy, a top-level heading absent from the document, and consecutive headings with no body content between them. The converter reads each heading level to construct the DITA map hierarchy, generating sub-maps, topic files, and topic type classifications from the heading sequence and the content that follows each heading.

conbody.p: A Headingstyle marks the beginning of a named section of content and assigns it a rank in the document hierarchy. It is the primary structural mechanism of any technical document — headings divide continuous content into discrete, named units, establish the parent-child relationships between those units, and create the navigational backbone that readers and publishing systems depend on.

The heading hierarchy is expressed through levels: a top-level heading (Heading 1) names a major section; each lower-level heading (Heading 2 through Heading N) names a subsection within its parent. This ranked sequence carries the same structural meaning regardless of the format it is expressed. The level communicates the section's position in the hierarchy; the text communicates its subject.
conbody.note: Only a semantically marked heading — applied through the document's native heading mechanism — creates a genuine section boundary that a converter, search engine, or publishing system can detect and act on.
conbody.p: In well-formed HTML, headings are applied sequentially without skipping levels. An <h1> is followed by one or more <h2> elements, each <h2> may contain one or more <h3> elements, and so on.

The converter reads the heading elements within the <body> of each HTML file to determine how many DITA topic files to generate, how to title and nest them in the Ditamap, and what topic type each one receives. It then analyzes the content that follows each heading, such as paragraphs, lists, and tables, to classify the resulting topic as Concept, Task, Reference, Troubleshooting, or Generic.
The following table shows how each HTML heading element maps to a DITA construct:

row.entry: The <Heading 1> text becomes both the Ditamap title and the primary topic title. Generates a .ditamap file and a corresponding .dita topic file.
A <topichead> element in the parent map. No DITA topic file is generated.
A child .ditamap file and a corresponding .dita topic file, referenced from the parent map.
A nested .ditamap file and a corresponding .dita topic file, referenced from the child map.
Additional nested .ditamap and .dita topic files at deeper nesting levels.

conbody.note: Never use <strong> or <b> elements to simulate headings. Bold text styled to look like a heading is not recognized as a structural marker. The content that follows it is added to the preceding topic. Use heading elements to define topic boundaries.
